children.name: Alca
children.description: Razorbills — medium-sized auks of the North Atlantic, named for the distinctive laterally compressed bill that is crossed with a white line. The razorbill (tordmule) is the closest living relative of the extinct great auk and shares its stocky, black-and-white coloration and awkward gait on land. In Sweden, razorbills breed on rocky sea cliffs on the west coast, particularly on Stora Karlsö off Gotland and at Nidingen on the Kattegat. Like all auks, razorbills are consummate underwater fliers, using their wings to pursue fish at depth. They are highly colonial breeders, choosing crevices and ledges in cliff faces rather than the open ledges preferred by guillemots.

children.name: Alca torda
children.description: The razorbill is a North Atlantic colonial seabird and the only extant member of the genus Alca of the family Alcidae, the auks. It is the closest living relative of the extinct great auk. Historically, it has also been known as "auk", "razor-billed auk" and "lesser auk".

children.name: Uria
children.description: Guillemots — the most abundant large seabirds in the North Atlantic, nesting in enormous cliff colonies that can contain hundreds of thousands of birds. The common guillemot (sillgrissla) breeds in one of the densest aggregations of any bird: pairs share tiny cliff ledges so tightly that incubating birds are pressed shoulder to shoulder in ranks, exchanging constant mutual preening and loud guttural calls. Guillemots lay a single pear-shaped egg directly on the bare rock — the tapering shape means it rolls in a tight circle rather than off the ledge. Chicks jump from the colony to the sea before they can fly, at around three weeks old, and are tended at sea by the father. Sweden's guillemot colonies, concentrated on limestone stacks off Gotland and the Kattegat archipelago, are among the most important seabird sites in the Baltic region.

children.name: Uria aalge
children.description: The common murre or common guillemot is a large auk, one of several species called murre or guillemot. It has a circumpolar distribution, occurring in low-Arctic and boreal waters in the North Atlantic and North Pacific. It spends most of its time at sea, only coming to land to breed on rocky cliff shores or islands.

children.name: Uria lomvia
children.description: The thick-billed murre or Brünnich's guillemot (Uria lomvia) is a bird in the auk family (Alcidae). This bird is named after the Danish zoologist Morten Thrane Brünnich. The very deeply black North Pacific subspecies Uria lomvia arra is also called Pallas' murre after its describer.

children.name: Cepphus
children.description: Black guillemots — smaller, rounder auks that differ fundamentally from their relatives in breeding close inshore, in small dispersed groups rather than large colonies, and in remaining in their breeding areas year-round rather than migrating to open ocean. The black guillemot (tobisgrissla) is one of the most characteristic birds of the Swedish outer archipelago, breeding under boulders and in rock crevices on skerry islands throughout the Baltic and Kattegat coasts. In breeding plumage it is entirely jet black with a large white wing patch and vivid scarlet feet and gape — one of the most striking of all Swedish seabirds. Its piping calls are a defining sound of the Swedish summer archipelago. Unlike other auks it dives primarily for bottom-dwelling fish and invertebrates in relatively shallow coastal waters.

children.name: Cepphus grylle
children.description:
The black guillemot or tystie (Cepphus grylle) is a medium-sized seabird of the Alcidae family, native throughout northern Atlantic coasts and eastern North American coasts. It is resident in much of its range, but large populations from the high arctic migrate southwards in winter. The bird can be seen in and around its breeding habitat of rocky shores, cliffs and islands in single or smalls groups of pairs. They feed mainly by diving towards the sea floor feeding on fish, crustaceans or other benthic invertebrates. They are listed on the IUCN red list as a species of least concern.
Both sexes have very similar appearances with black plumage and a large white patch on the upper side of their wings in summer. The bill is also black, being rather long and slender, while the feet are coral-red. In winter adult underparts are white and the upperparts are a pale grey with the back and shoulders exhibiting barred light grey and white patterning.

children.name: Cepphus columba
children.description: The pigeon guillemot (Cepphus columba) ( ) is a species of bird in the auk family, Alcidae.

children.name: Cepphus carbo
children.description: The spectacled guillemot or sooty guillemot (Cepphus carbo) is a seabird in the auk family.

children.name: Alle
children.description: Little auk — the smallest North Atlantic auk, barely larger than a starling yet one of the most abundant seabirds in the world, with breeding colonies in the High Arctic (particularly northwestern Greenland and Svalbard) numbering in the millions. The little auk (alkekung) is a highly pelagic bird, spending its non-breeding months far out in the North Atlantic and Barents Sea where it feeds on copepods and other tiny crustaceans. It very rarely approaches Swedish coasts voluntarily, but in years of severe autumn storms, exhausted and disoriented birds may be blown inland — 'wrecks' of little auks occasionally occur in Sweden when Atlantic gales sweep birds far from their usual pelagic range.

children.name: Alle alle
children.description: The little auk (Europe) or dovekie (North America) (Alle alle) is a small auk, the only member of the genus Alle.

children.name: Fratercula
children.description: Puffins — the most iconic and instantly recognisable of all the auks, beloved for their clown-like colourful bill and upright posture. The Atlantic puffin (lunnefågel) breeds in burrows excavated in soft coastal turf on offshore islands. In Sweden, the main breeding sites are on Nidingen and Hallands Väderö off the Kattegat coast — the easternmost significant puffin colonies in Europe. Sweden's puffin population is small and has declined sharply since the mid-20th century, making each individual a precious sight. Puffins carry multiple sand eels crosswise in the bill simultaneously (using backward-facing serrations to hold earlier catches while catching more) — some individuals have been recorded carrying over 60 fish in a single bill-load.

children.name: Fratercula arctica
children.description: The Atlantic puffin, also known as the common puffin, is a species of seabird in the auk family. It is the only puffin native to the Atlantic Ocean; two related species, the tufted puffin and the horned puffin, are found in the northeastern Pacific. The Atlantic puffin breeds in Russia, Iceland, Ireland, Britain, Norway, Greenland, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, and the Faroe Islands, and as far south as Maine in the west and France in the east.

children.name: Fratercula cirrhata
children.description: The tufted puffin (Fratercula cirrhata), also known as crested puffin, is a relatively abundant medium-sized pelagic seabird in the auk family (Alcidae) found throughout the North Pacific Ocean.

children.name: Fratercula corniculata
children.description: The horned puffin (Fratercula corniculata) is an auk found in the North Pacific Ocean, including the coasts of Alaska, Siberia and British Columbia.

children.name: Brachyramphus
children.description: Murrelets of the North Pacific — small, cryptically patterned auks with a unique nesting habit: they do not breed in colonies but lay eggs singly on the mossy branches of old-growth trees or on remote alpine scree, far from the sea. The Marbled Murrelet's dependence on coastal old-growth forest has made it a flagship species for Pacific Northwest forest conservation.

children.name: Brachyramphus marmoratus
children.description: The marbled murrelet (Brachyramphus marmoratus) is a small seabird from the North Pacific.

children.name: Brachyramphus perdix
children.description:
The long-billed murrelet (Brachyramphus perdix) is a small seabird from the North Pacific. The genus name Brachyramphus is from Ancient Greek brakhus, "short", and rhamphos, "bill". The species name perdix is Latin for "partridge" Pallas described this auk as Magnitudine Perdicis. "Murrelet" is a diminutive of "murre", a word of uncertain origins, but which may imitate the call of the common guillemot.
This auk is an unusual member of the auk family, often nesting far inland in old growth forests. The long-billed murrelet, like its cousins the marbled and Kittlitz's murrelets, is thought to have experienced a decline in numbers recently.

children.name: Brachyramphus brevirostris
children.description:
Kittlitz's murrelet (Brachyramphus brevirostris) is a small alcid found in the waters off Alaska and Eastern Siberia. This near threatened species is, like the closely related marbled murrelet, unusual for seabirds in not being colonial, nesting instead in isolated locations on mountain tops, where the nests were known to Native Americans for many years before skeptical ornithologists described and photographed them. It is a poorly known and little studied species, although concern over its status and that of the closely related marbled murrelet has led to a recent increase in research.
The common name of this species commemorates the German zoologist Heinrich von Kittlitz, who first collected this species.

children.name: Synthliboramphus
children.description: The ancient murrelets of the North Pacific — small auks that fly from the colony to the open ocean within days of hatching, never returning to land until they breed. They are the most precocial of all seabirds: chicks jump from the nest on the second night after hatching and follow their parents out to sea, swimming and diving from the first moment.

children.name: Synthliboramphus antiquus
children.description: The ancient murrelet () is a bird in the auk family.

children.name: Synthliboramphus wumizusume
children.description: The Japanese murrelet or crested murrelet (Synthliboramphus wumizusume) is a small seabird in the auk family that occurs along the remote rocky coasts and in the offshore waters of Japan, and may also be found after the breeding season as far as Sakhalin to the north and in particular off South Korea. With a small and declining population, estimated as of 2017 to total 2,500–10,000 individuals, it is the rarest alcid, and the most at risk of extinction.

children.name: Synthliboramphus craveri
children.description: Craveri's murrelet (Synthliboramphus craveri) is a small seabird which breeds on offshore islands in both the Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of California off the Baja peninsula of Mexico. It also wanders fairly regularly as far as central California in the US, primarily during post-breeding dispersal. It is almost never seen from or near the shore. With an estimated population of 6,000-10,000 breeding pairs, its population is listed as vulnerable.

children.name: Synthliboramphus hypoleucus
children.description: The Guadalupe murrelet (Synthliboramphus hypoleucus) or Xantus's murrelet is a small seabird found in the California Current system in the Pacific Ocean.

children.name: Synthliboramphus scrippsi
children.description:
Scripps's murrelet (Synthliboramphus scrippsi) is a small seabird found in the California Current system in the Pacific Ocean. This auk breeds on islands off California and Mexico. It is threatened by predators introduced to its breeding colonies and by oil spills.
This species and the Guadalupe murrelet were considered conspecific and were known collectively as Xantus's murrelet until 2012. The two species are now considered distinct based on a lack of evidence of interbreeding at a shared nesting colony on the San Benito Islands, differences in facial pattern and bill shape, and differences in vocalizations and genetics.

children.name: Ptychoramphus
children.description: A monotypic genus containing Cassin's Auklet — a small, stubby-billed auklet of the North Pacific that is one of the most abundant seabirds on the California Current system. It nests in burrows on offshore islands and is an important indicator of ocean health for fisheries management.

children.name: Ptychoramphus aleuticus
children.description:
Cassin's auklet (Ptychoramphus aleuticus) is a small, chunky seabird that ranges widely in the North Pacific. It is the only species placed in the genus Ptychoramphus. It nests in small burrows and because of its presence on well studied islands in British Columbia and off California it is one of the better known auks. It is named for the American ornithologist John Cassin.
Cassin's auklet is a small (25 cm, 200 g) nondescript auk. Its plumage is generally dark above and pale below, with a small white mark above the eye. Its bill is overall dark with a pale spot, and its feet are blue. Unlike many other auks, Cassin's auklet lacks dramatic breeding plumage, remaining the same over most of the year. At sea it is usually identified by its flight, which is described as looking like a flying tennis ball.

children.name: Aethia
children.description: The four smallest auklets — tiny seabirds of the North Pacific that breed in immense colonies on volcanic islands, often alongside each other. They are adorned with a remarkable array of facial plumes and horny plates used in courtship displays. The Least Auklet at 85 g is the smallest of all alcids, while the Crested Auklet has a forward-curving forehead crest and produces a strong citrus-like scent during the breeding season.

children.name: Aethia psittacula
children.description: The parakeet auklet (Aethia psittacula) is a small seabird of the North Pacific.

children.name: Aethia pusilla
children.description: The least auklet (Aethia pusilla) is a seabird and the smallest species of auk.

children.name: Aethia pygmaea
children.description: The whiskered auklet is a small seabird of the auk family. It has a more restricted range than other members of its genus, Aethia, living only around the Aleutian Islands and on some islands off Siberia, and breeding on these islands. It is one of the smallest alcids, only the closely related least auklet being smaller.

children.name: Aethia cristatella
children.description: The crested auklet is a small seabird of the family Alcidae, distributed throughout the northern Pacific and the Bering Sea. The species feeds by diving in deep waters, eating krill and a variety of small marine animals. It nests in dense colonies of up to 1 million individuals in the Bering Sea and the Sea of Okhotsk.

children.name: Cerorhinca
children.description: A monotypic genus containing the Rhinoceros Auklet — a puffin-like auk that is the closest living relative of the puffins. It is named for the horny 'rhinoceros-like' projection at the base of the bill in breeding season. Despite its name it is larger and heavier than any true auklet, approaching the size of a small puffin.

children.name: Cerorhinca monocerata
children.description: The rhinoceros auklet (Cerorhinca monocerata) is a seabird and a close relative of the puffins.

children.name: Pinguinus
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Great Auk — the largest of all auks and the only one entirely flightless, rendered vulnerable by its inability to fly and ruthlessly exterminated by 19th-century hunters for its feathers, meat, and oil. The last breeding pair was killed on Eldey Island, Iceland, in 1844, and the last confirmed individual was seen on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland in 1852. The Great Auk is one of the most iconic species extinctions of the modern era.

children.name: Pinguinus impennis
children.description: The great auk (Pinguinus impennis), also known as the garefowl or penguin, is an extinct species of flightless alcid that first appeared around 400,000 years ago and was driven to extinction by human exploitation in the mid-19th century.
